title: a procedure anyone can run at home, containing no stored figure at all
why: The cleanest demonstration of the whole idea, and the easiest for a stranger to try. The correct pressure is printed on the side of the tyre, so a good procedure does not carry a number — it carries an instruction to read one off the machine and an acceptance rule that resolves against it. If the Scoper writes a bound like 40 psi here it has invented a figure for a tyre it has never seen, and every rider following it over-inflates something.

shop.trade: one person looking after their own ride at home, no workshop
shop.machines: a Segway Xyber e-bike, plus a couple of ordinary bicycles
shop.stakes: it gets ridden in city traffic and on gravel; a brake or a tyre letting go at speed puts the rider under a car

facts.what the job is: check and pump up both tyres before a ride, front and back
facts.how I know what pressure to use: it's moulded into the sidewall of the tyre itself, there's a max pressure printed right there and I go to that. Every tyre is different so I always read the one in front of me
facts.how I check: a pump with a gauge on it, or a separate pressure gauge if the pump hasn't got one
facts.what I do first: have a proper look at the tyre for anything stuck in it, glass or a thorn, before I put air in
facts.what stops the job: if the tyre's cracked or the sidewall is split I don't pump it up at all, that tyre needs replacing not inflating
facts.evidence I keep: photo of the gauge reading and a photo of the sidewall so you can see the number I was aiming for
